subject: biology-hl
author: original (NevaIB)
title: Inheritance
bigPicture: Each parent passes on one allele of every gene. Dominant, recessive, codominant and sex-linked alleles give predictable ratios that Punnett grids and pedigrees can predict. HL extends this to two genes at once, linkage, recombinants and testing results with chi-squared.

keyIdeas.cue: How are genes inherited in a sexual life cycle?
keyIdeas.answer: Each parent makes haploid gametes; fusion gives a diploid zygote with two copies of every autosomal gene, one from each parent. This is common to all sexually reproducing eukaryotes.

keyIdeas.cue: How are genetic crosses done in plants?
keyIdeas.answer: Transfer pollen (male gametes) to the stigma of a chosen plant; female gametes are in the ovary. Peas can self-fertilise, so for a cross the anthers are removed and pollen transferred by hand. Terms: P (parents), F1 (first offspring), F2 (offspring of F1), Punnett grid. Crosses are widely used to breed new crop and ornamental varieties.

keyIdeas.cue: Gene vs allele; homozygous vs heterozygous?
keyIdeas.answer: A gene is a heritable factor at a particular locus; alleles are its alternative forms. Homozygous: two identical alleles. Heterozygous: two different alleles. Genotype is the combination of alleles.

keyIdeas.cue: What decides phenotype?
keyIdeas.answer: Genotype and environment. Genotype only: ABO blood group, eye colour. Environment only: scars, language spoken. Both: height, skin colour (genes plus nutrition or sun exposure).

keyIdeas.cue: Why do AA and Aa have the same phenotype?
keyIdeas.answer: The dominant allele usually codes for a functional protein; one copy makes enough product. The recessive allele (often non-functional) only shows when there's no dominant allele.

keyIdeas.cue: What is phenotypic plasticity?
keyIdeas.answer: An organism developing traits suited to its environment by changing gene expression, not genotype, e.g. tanning, muscle growth with training, leaf shape in sun vs shade. Changes may be reversible.

keyIdeas.cue: What causes phenylketonuria?
keyIdeas.answer: A recessive allele of an autosomal gene for the enzyme that converts phenylalanine to tyrosine. Homozygous recessive people build up phenylalanine, which harms brain development unless they follow a low-phenylalanine diet.

keyIdeas.cue: How many alleles can a gene have?
keyIdeas.answer: Any number can exist in the gene pool (new SNPs keep arising), but each diploid individual carries only two.

keyIdeas.cue: How is ABO blood group inherited?
keyIdeas.answer: Three alleles: Iᴬ and Iᴮ are codominant, and both are dominant to i. Group A: IᴬIᴬ or Iᴬi; B: IᴮIᴮ or Iᴮi; AB: IᴬIᴮ; O: ii.

keyIdeas.cue: Codominance vs incomplete dominance?
keyIdeas.answer: Codominance: the heterozygote shows both phenotypes (blood group AB). Incomplete dominance: the heterozygote has an intermediate phenotype (red × white four o'clock flower, Mirabilis jalapa, gives pink).

keyIdeas.cue: How is sex determined in humans?
keyIdeas.answer: Females XX, males XY. Eggs always carry X; the sperm's X or Y decides the zygote's sex, since the Y chromosome triggers male-typical development. The X carries far more genes than the Y.

keyIdeas.cue: How is haemophilia inherited?
keyIdeas.answer: Recessive allele on the X chromosome (Xʰ). Males have one X, so XʰY has haemophilia. Females need XʰXʰ; XᴴXʰ women are carriers. Affected sons inherit it from their mothers.

keyIdeas.cue: How do you analyse a pedigree chart?
keyIdeas.answer: Squares = male, circles = female, shaded = affected (symbols in the data booklet). Two unaffected parents with an affected child means recessive. Mostly affected males inherited through carrier mothers suggests X-linked. Close relatives are more likely to carry the same recessive alleles, which is why many societies forbid marriage between them.

keyIdeas.cue: What causes continuous variation?
keyIdeas.answer: Polygenic inheritance (many genes each adding a small effect) and/or environment, e.g. skin colour. Continuous variables vary across a range (use mean, median, mode); discrete ones fall into categories (ABO group).

keyIdeas.cue: What does a box-and-whisker plot show?
keyIdeas.answer: Minimum, lower quartile (Q1), median, upper quartile (Q3), maximum, and outliers: points more than 1.5 × IQR below Q1 or above Q3 (IQR = Q3 − Q1).

keyIdeas.cue: How does meiosis explain segregation and independent assortment?
keyIdeas.answer: The two alleles of a gene separate into different gametes (segregation) because homologues separate in meiosis I. Genes on different chromosomes assort independently because each bivalent orients randomly at metaphase I.

keyIdeas.cue: Where do the 9:3:3:1 and 1:1:1:1 ratios come from?
keyIdeas.answer: AaBb × AaBb: each parent makes AB, Ab, aB, ab equally; a 4×4 grid gives 9 A_B_ : 3 A_bb : 3 aaB_ : 1 aabb. AaBb × aabb (test cross) gives 1:1:1:1. Valid only for unlinked genes (Mendel's second law).

keyIdeas.cue: What does a gene database show about loci?
keyIdeas.answer: Each gene has a locus on a chromosome and a polypeptide product. Databases show some gene pairs on different chromosomes and others close together on the same chromosome.

keyIdeas.cue: What is gene linkage?
keyIdeas.answer: Genes close together on the same chromosome tend to be inherited together because they don't assort independently. Write linked genotypes with alleles beside vertical lines for each homologue, e.g. AB | ab.

keyIdeas.cue: What are recombinants?
keyIdeas.answer: Offspring with combinations of alleles not found in either parent. In AaBb × aabb, unlinked genes give 50% recombinants. Linked genes give mostly parental types and only a few recombinants, from crossing over.

keyIdeas.cue: How is chi-squared used for dihybrid crosses?
keyIdeas.answer: Null hypothesis: the results fit the expected ratio (e.g. 9:3:3:1). χ² = Σ(O−E)²/E, df = categories − 1 (3 for four classes, critical value 7.81 at p = 0.05). If χ² is above the critical value, reject the null; a significant deviation may indicate linkage.

keyTerms.def: Both alleles expressed in the heterozygote.
Gene carried on a sex chromosome (usually X).
Genes on the same chromosome inherited together.
Offspring with a new combination of parental alleles.

workedExamples.title: Haemophilia cross
workedExamples.prompt: A carrier woman and an unaffected man have children. Predict the outcomes.
steps: Gametes: Xᴴ, Xʰ and Xᴴ, Y.
workedExamples.answer: Daughters: 50% carriers, none affected. Sons: 50% chance of haemophilia.

workedExamples.title: Chi-squared on a dihybrid cross (AHL)
workedExamples.prompt: Expected 9:3:3:1 from 160 F2 plants; observed 94, 30, 28, 8. Test the fit.
workedExamples.answer: 0.71 < 7.81: accept the null; the results fit a 9:3:3:1 ratio.

misconceptions.right: Blending is incomplete dominance; codominance shows both.

misconceptions.wrong: Men can be carriers of haemophilia.
misconceptions.right: Men with the allele are affected; only women are carriers.
